title_en: Beijing Ciwen Film and Television Production Co., Ltd. v. China Netcom Group Corporation (Hainan Branch) — copyright infringement dispute
ruling_gist_en: First, where an internet service provider sets up a "video channel" on the homepage of a website it operates, and users can view movies copyrighted by others by clicking to enter the relevant page and performing operations, and the domain name, website name, and other information displayed on the relevant page do not indicate that the webpage belongs to a third party, if the internet service provider claims that the webpage is a third-party website to which it links, it shall bear the burden of proof.

full_text_en:
Beijing Ciwen Film and Television Production Co., Ltd. v. China Netcom Group Corporation Hainan Province Branch — dispute over copyright infringement

Ruling Summary

1. Where an Internet service provider sets up a "movie channel" on the homepage of its website, and users can click to enter relevant pages and perform operations to view a film in which others hold copyright, and the information displayed on the relevant pages, such as the domain name and website name, does not indicate that the web page belongs to a third party, the Internet service provider, if it claims that the web page is linked to a third-party website, shall bear the burden of proof.

2. Under the above circumstances, even if the web page to which the "movie channel" directs is indeed owned or actually operated by a third party, because the Internet service provider provides the content of that web page to the public as a column of its own website, its conduct differs from providing an ordinary link to a third-party website. The Internet service provider also has a certain duty of care with respect to the content involved. If it fails to fulfill such duty of care, it shall bear joint and several liability for the act of infringing upon the copyright of others.

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court

(2009) Min Ti Zi No. 17

Applicant for Retrial (Plaintiff at First Instance, Appellant at Second Instance): Beijing Ciwen Film and Television Production Co., Ltd., domiciled at No. 89, Shaling Section, Shunping Road, Yangzhen Area, Shunyi District, Beijing.

Legal Representative: Ma Zhongjun, Chairman of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Zhuang Jianbing, lawyer of Shanghai Tianwen Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Sun Liqing, lawyer of Shanghai Tianwen Law Firm.

Respondent (Defendant at First Instance, Appellee at Second Instance): China Netcom Group Corporation Hainan Province Branch, domiciled at Floors 30-32, Block A, CCB Building, No. 8 Guomao Avenue, Haikou City, Hainan Province.

Legal Representative: Dai Bin, General Manager of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Li Jian, staff member of the Company.

Agent ad litem: Xia Xiaohua, staff member of the Company.

The applicant for retrial, Beijing Ciwen Film and Television Production Co., Ltd. (referred to as "Ciwen Company"), due to a dispute over copyright infringement with China Netcom Group Corporation Hainan Province Branch (referred to as "Hainan Netcom Company"), dissatisfied with the civil judgment (2006) Qiong Min Er Zhong Zi No. 29 rendered by the Hainan High People's Court on September 25, 2006, applied to this Court for a retrial. This Court rendered the civil ruling (2007) Min San Jian Zi No. 44-1 on December 16, 2008, granting the retrial of this case. This Court formed a collegiate panel according to law to hear this case, and the trial has now been concluded.

On December 16, 2005, the plaintiff at first instance, Ciwen Company, filed a lawsuit with the Haikou Intermediate People's Court, alleging that Ciwen Company owned the copyright to the film "Seven Swords," and that Hainan Netcom Company, by providing online streaming services of the film to the public on its website www.hai169.com, infringed upon Ciwen Company's copyright. Ciwen Company requested the court to order Hainan Netcom Company to immediately cease the infringement, issue an apology, and compensate for economic losses of 200,000 yuan and reasonable expenses of 30,000 yuan. Hainan Netcom Company argued in its defense that it had not engaged in the unauthorized dissemination of the film in question, that the website streaming the film was http://221.11.132.112, and that Hainan Netcom Company only provided a linking service and had already severed the link after Ciwen Company filed the lawsuit, so it should not bear liability for infringement.

The Haikou Intermediate People's Court found at first instance that Ciwen Company owned the copyright to the film "Seven Swords" in the mainland region. The notarial certificate (2005) Hu Jing Zheng Jing Zi No. 4758 issued by the Shanghai Jing'an District Notary Public Office, submitted by Ciwen Company, showed that on September 19, 2005, upon entering the website www.hai169.com of Hainan Netcom Company and clicking on the "Movie Channel" on the homepage, one entered "Film World" (IP address 221.11.132.112). By entering "Seven Swords" in the search bar and sequentially clicking "Search," "Details and Introduction," "Watch Online Side A," and "Watch Online Side B," an introduction to the film and the entire film work could be viewed. The screen that appeared after clicking "Watch Online Side A" displayed: "Jointly produced by Beijing Ciwen Film and Television Production Co., Ltd., Mandarin Films Production Company, and Huaying Film Co., Ltd."

The notarial certificate (2006) Qiong Er Zheng Zi No. 647 issued by the Hainan Province Second Notary Public Office, submitted by Hainan Netcom Company, showed that on February 9, 2006, upon entering the homepage of www.hai169.com and clicking the "Movie Channel" at the top of the homepage, one entered the "116 Tiantian Online" webpage instead of the original "Film World" webpage.

Ciwen Company paid notarial fees of 1,000 yuan and attorney fees of 30,000 yuan.

The Haikou Intermediate People's Court held at first instance that, from a technical perspective, Hainan Netcom Company's website merely guided Ciwen Company to the source information website through a linking function. Hainan Netcom Company did not store the work "Seven Swords" on its own server to provide online streaming services to the public, and the existing evidence could not prove that the webpage containing the work "Seven Swords" was established by Hainan Netcom Company. Hainan Netcom Company's linking conduct did not infringe Ciwen Company's copyright. Moreover, after being accused of infringement, it had promptly severed the link, thereby preventing the expansion of the infringing consequences. Therefore, Hainan Netcom Company should not bear civil liability for infringement for playing the work that infringed Ciwen Company's copyright. On May 8, 2006, the Haikou Intermediate People's Court rendered the civil judgment (2006) Hai Zhong Fa Min San Chu Zi No. 2: dismissing Ciwen Company's claims.

Ciwen Company, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Hainan High People's Court, requesting the reversal of the first-instance judgment and support for all its claims at first instance. Hainan Netcom Company agreed with the first-instance judgment.

The Hainan High People's Court confirmed the facts found at first instance at the second instance.

The Hainan High People's Court held at the second instance that the evidence in this case indicated that Hainan Netcom Company was an Internet service provider offering linking services. Although the IP address of the page containing the film "Seven Swords" belonged to Hainan Netcom Company, this only proved that the IP user was one of over 20,000 users of Hainan Netcom Company. It could not be inferred from this that the webpage was established by Hainan Netcom Company, let alone that Hainan Netcom Company was an Internet service provider offering content services, thereby bearing liability for infringement. An Internet service provider cannot be expected to review one by one the specific circumstances and content of a vast number of website users, nor does it have the obligation to determine the legality of such content. The reason given by Ciwen Company that Hainan Netcom Company and the allegedly infringing website were jointly infringing and should bear joint and several liability lacked factual and legal basis and was not adopted. The Hainan High People's Court rendered the judgment: dismissing the appeal and affirming the original judgment.

Ciwen Company applied for retrial, arguing: First, the facts found by the two lower courts were unclear. The "Film World" where the film was specifically played was a secondary channel of Hainan Netcom Company's website. It had no ordinary domain name, only an IP address, which fell within the range of IP addresses managed by Hainan Netcom Company. Hainan Netcom Company should have provided information on the actual user of that IP address but refused to do so. Moreover, after Hainan Netcom Company responded to the lawsuit at first instance, neither www.hai169.com nor its "Film World" website could be viewed normally, proving that Hainan Netcom Company had control over the "Film World" website. The evidence submitted by Hainan Netcom Company could not prove that the network dissemination act was carried out by a third-party website it linked to. Second, the application of law by the two lower courts was erroneous. Hainan Netcom Company was not a simple Internet service provider in this case but should be considered a content provider, and the provisions concerning "safe harbor" should not apply. Third, the determination of liability by the two lower courts was improper and led to adverse consequences. In summary, Ciwen Company requested the reversal of the original judgments and support for its claims at first instance.

Hainan Netcom Company argued in defense: The facts found by the two lower courts were clear, and the application of law was correct. The allegedly infringing website was http://221.11.132.112, and Hainan Netcom Company's website only provided a link to that website. Although the IP address fell within the IP address range managed by Hainan Netcom Company, it could not be concluded that the infringing website was established and operated by Hainan Netcom Company. In this case, Hainan Netcom Company only provided a linking service from its own website to the allegedly infringing website; it was an Internet service provider, not a content provider. The allegedly infringing IP user was one of Hainan Netcom Company's 24,480 users. Hainan Netcom Company could not review the vast number of websites one by one, and after learning that the linked website was allegedly infringing, it had promptly taken measures to sever the link, so it should not bear liability. It requested the affirmation of the original judgments.

This Court confirmed at the retrial that the facts found by the original courts were true.

This Court held at the retrial: Ciwen Company owns the copyright to the film "Seven Swords" in the mainland region and should be protected according to law. Anyone who, without permission, disseminates the film work to the public through an information network shall bear corresponding legal liability. In this case, the notarial certificate submitted by Ciwen Company showed that by accessing Hainan Netcom Company's website through the Internet and clicking on the "Movie Channel" on its homepage, one could operate on the page entered to view the film "Seven Swords." Although the entered webpage had the name "Film World," no corresponding domain name or website name information was displayed on that webpage to indicate that the webpage belonged to a third party. The IP address of that webpage could not prove that the webpage belonged to another subject. Therefore, from the perspective of Ciwen Company and the general public, the webpage playing the film "Seven Swords" at least ostensibly belonged to Hainan Netcom Company. If Hainan Netcom Company wished to prove that the webpage was only a third-party website it linked to and that it should not bear liability for the infringement on that webpage, it should submit corresponding evidence. Because the IP address of that webpage fell within the address range managed by Hainan Netcom Company, Hainan Netcom Company could provide that evidence, while the general public, including Ciwen Company, could not obtain it. In the absence of relevant evidence provided by Hainan Netcom Company, its defense that it only provided a linking service could not be sustained, and it should bear corresponding legal liability for the act of infringement on that webpage of playing the film work in which Ciwen Company owns the copyright. Even if the webpage was indeed owned or actually operated by a third party, since the "Movie Channel" was listed alongside Hainan Netcom Company's website "Homepage," "News Channel," "Literature Channel," etc., and Hainan Netcom Company provided the content of that webpage to the public as one of its content channels, and considering that the notarial certificate it submitted in the original trial showed that the content of the "Movie Channel" was changed after being sued, this choice was entirely made independently by Hainan Netcom Company. Therefore, this conduct differs from providing an ordinary link to a third-party website. Hainan Netcom Company also has a certain duty to review the content on this channel, and it should at least conduct some review of the qualification of the actual owner or operator of the website. In this case, Hainan Netcom Company has stated to this day that it did not know the actual operator of the webpage, thus failing to fulfill the minimum duty of care. It should also bear joint and several liability for the infringement appearing on that webpage. In summary, the determination by the original courts that Hainan Netcom Company only provided a linking service and that disconnecting the link upon learning of the infringement would exempt it from liability was improper, and this Court corrects it. Hainan Netcom Company shall bear civil liability, including ceasing the infringement and compensating for losses, for the act of infringing upon Ciwen Company's right of communication through information networks.

Since Hainan Netcom Company, after Ciwen Company filed the lawsuit, had already changed the content of the "Movie Channel" column on its website, meaning it had stopped the online streaming of "Seven Swords," it is no longer necessary to order it to cease the infringement. Regarding compensation for losses, because Ciwen Company did not submit evidence to prove the losses it suffered from the infringement, and the profits Hainan Netcom Company obtained from the act cannot be determined, this Court, based on factors such as the duration the film "Seven Swords" existed on its website, the film's release date and influence, and considering the reasonable expenses Ciwen Company incurred for this case, determines that Hainan Netcom Company shall compensate Ciwen Company for economic losses of 80,000 yuan. Ciwen Company also requested an apology. Because the webpage in question playing the film "Seven Swords" displayed the content that Ciwen Company and others jointly produced the film, Ciwen Company's right of attribution or other personal rights were not infringed, so this Court does not support Ciwen Company's claim in this regard.

In conclusion, pursuant to Article 186, Paragraph 1, and Article 153, Paragraph 1, Item (2) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 47, Item (1) of the Copyright Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 3 of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Application of Law in Trials of Copyright Disputes Involving Computer Networks, the judgment is as follows:

1. The civil judgment (2006) Qiong Min Er Zhong Zi No. 29 of the Hainan High People's Court and the civil judgment (2006) Hai Zhong Fa Min San Chu Zi No. 2 of the Haikou Intermediate People's Court are reversed;

2. Within 10 days from the date this judgment takes effect, China Netcom Group Corporation Hainan Province Branch shall compensate Beijing Ciwen Film and Television Production Co., Ltd. for economic losses of RMB 80,000 (including reasonable expenses incurred for the lawsuit);

3. The other claims of Beijing Ciwen Film and Television Production Co., Ltd. are dismissed.

If the obligation to pay money is not fulfilled within the period specified in this judgment, the debt interest for delayed payment shall be doubled in accordance with Article 229 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China.

The case acceptance fees for the first instance and second instance are each 5,960 yuan, both to be borne by China Netcom Group Corporation Hainan Province Branch (to be paid within seven days from the date this judgment takes effect).

This judgment is final.

Presiding Judge: Yu Xiaobai
Judge: Yin Shaoping
Judge: Xia Junli

April 28, 2009
